 Credit: Far Out / YouTube Still In 1994, Martin Short made the worst movie of his career. It was inspired by the “most perverse” film he’d ever seen
 Scott Campbell November 1st, 2026 · 9:45pm GMT Follow us on Google Discover Whenever an actor makes an objectively terrible movie, they’re allowed to defend it to the death as a misunderstood masterpiece, even if they don’t have a leg to stand on. Martin Short has been doing it for years, but more and more people are starting to come around to his way of thinking.
 Obviously, that doesn’t instantly turn an awful film into a good one. Look at Tommy Wiseau’s The Room ; by any conventional standards of taste, tone, directorial skill, and acting ability, it’s a fucking atrocious work of cinema. And yet, that’s the exact reason why so many people love it so dearly.
 It takes a special kind of bad movie to find a new life as a ‘so bad it’s good’ cult classic, but that’s what’s happened to Short’s 1995 effort, Clifford . It’s crap, and even its staunchest defenders have no other choice than to admit it, but it’s so crap that it’s come back around again to become a firm cult favourite.
 Roger Ebert thought it was horrendous, and it was, but Nicolas Cage watched it so many times that his VHS copy almost crumbled into dust, but you’d expect him to be part of the fan club, because he’s a weirdo . As for Short, he drew his inspiration from the most unlikely of places.
 In Clifford , despite being 44 years old when production commenced, he plays a ten-year-old boy, which is the joke, as you’d guess. Despite being roundly savaged as one of the year’s worst pictures, which it was, the leading man is one of the many who believe it never got the flowers it was due .
 The plot, if you can call it that, follows the title character and the misadventures that befall him and his relatives when the ‘youngster’ goes to stay with his uncle. Even though it’s supposed to be a comedy, Short admitted he was most influenced by the 1956 horror/mystery hybrid, The Bad Seed .
 “I’d seen that film a million times,” he explained. “That was one of the most perverse films in the world. I think what was inspired by The Bad Seed was the idea of the nonstop, obsessive nature of getting what you wanted, at any cost.” Looking at the two films, you can definitely see the shared DNA, to an extent.

 Patty McCormack was Academy Award-nominated as ‘Best Supporting Actress’ for her performance as Rhoda Penmark, a cherubic eight-year-old whose mother gradually begins to suspect that her daughter might be a calculating, cold-blooded murderer, and she’s bang on the money .
 Using her as one of his touchstones, Short used it to inform his own turn in Clifford . As the then-president of Orion Pictures, Marc Platt, recalled, “That’s either the greatest idea in the world or the worst idea in the world.” As it turned out, it was a little bit of both, depending on how you feel about the movie.
